name: Lemon and sugar lip lightening

lead: Some people rub lemon juice, often mixed with sugar, onto their lips hoping to lighten them and slough off dry skin for a smoother, lighter look.
Proponents credit the acidity of lemon, which is about 5 to 6 percent citric acid, and the abrasion of sugar. No published study of the mixture for lip pigmentation was identified.

paras: It is a home routine: juice and sugar are mixed, rubbed gently on the lips and rinsed off, usually repeated over days or weeks. People often follow it with a lip balm.

Contact with citrus juice followed by sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis, with redness, blistering and lasting brown marks, because plant compounds such as furanocoumarins sensitize skin to UVA. Lips are thin skin, and lemon acid can sting on chapped or cracked areas.

angle.text: DIY posters rub lemon juice and sugar on the lips hoping to lighten them. The idea is that the acid fades pigment while the sugar exfoliates, leaving lighter lips. It is a home-remedy belief, and no study has looked at it for lip color.

lead: Lemon and sugar lip lightening is a home remedy in which lemon juice, usually mixed with sugar granules, is applied to or gently rubbed on the lips with the aim of making darker lips look lighter and smoother. People try it for an even, pinker or softer-looking lip colour. Proponents attribute the effect to the acidity of lemon juice and to the mild abrasion of sugar acting as an exfoliant.

Lip colour comes from the thin lip skin, which has three to five cellular layers compared with up to sixteen on typical facial skin and fewer melanocytes, so blood vessels show through and give the lips their red tone; people with more melanin show this effect less [1]. Healthline lists darker lips as usually harmless hyperpigmentation with triggers including sun exposure, dehydration, smoking, allergic reactions to products such as toothpaste or lipstick, and lip sucking [2]. It also describes lemon-juice rubs and a lemon-and-sugar rub as home remedies, citing a 2002 study suggesting citrus peel may inhibit melanin, while noting that evidence is limited and more research is needed for sugar-based remedies [2].

Lemon juice is about 5 to 6 percent citric acid [3]. Dermatology references describe phytophotodermatitis, a reaction in which light-sensitising plant compounds called furanocoumarins on the skin plus UVA exposure cause inflammation and later pigmentation; lime is the best-known source and the Wikipedia article does not name lemon [4].

paras: Proponents describe gentle scrubbing of the lips with the mixture and rinsing afterwards. Lip skin is very thin, with three to five cell layers versus up to sixteen on typical facial skin, and it has no hair or sweat glands and lacks the oil layer that keeps other skin smooth, so lips dry out and chap faster than other skin [1].

Healthline attributes dark lips mostly to hyperpigmentation, an excess of melanin, from sun exposure, dehydration, smoking, product allergies, caffeine and lip sucking, and notes that chemotherapy, anemia, vitamin deficiencies and excess fluoride can contribute [2]. It suggests sunscreen and treating the underlying cause, and advises talking with a doctor [2].

Phytophotodermatitis follows skin contact with a light-sensitising botanical followed by sunlight. Symptoms appear within about a day, peak at 48 to 72 hours, and can include redness, burning and blisters; healing may leave brown or purplish marks that can last several years [4]. The Wikipedia article names lime as the best-known source and does not mention lemon, so the link to lemon juice comes from the same furanocoumarin mechanism rather than from that page [4]. Consumer sites advise rinsing off lemon and avoiding sun afterward because of photosensitivity, and note that citrus can sting on cracked lips.

No studies found for lemon and sugar on lip colour. The nearest cited research is a 2002 study that suggested citrus peel may inhibit melanin, referenced by Healthline, which is not a test of lemon juice on lips [2].
